page.title: A million ants in your browser
page.description: Two anthills in a browser tab, where every ant and queen is a tinyactors actor running on WebAssembly.

hero.headline: A million actors in this tab.
hero.lede: Every ant and queen is a statechart running on tinyactors in your browser. An ant uses the CPU only while it handles a message.

section.heading: Messages decide how many ants keep up.
section.p: The world tells an ant when it reaches food or home, and that message is the ant's next event. While the ant walks, it waits in memory and your GPU draws it.
Shorter rests mean more messages a second. The time per message stays level as you add ants, and the real-time chart shows whether your device keeps up.

playground.description: Two anthills on a field. Workers carry food home to their queen, and workers of the two colonies fight where they meet.

section.heading: An ant is a statechart.
section.p: An egg becomes a larva and then a worker, which forages until an event ends it. The world sends die when the ant grows old.

section.heading: So is a queen.
section.p: Once a second she lays an egg for every two pieces of food her workers brought home.

section.heading: Charts send messages to the world.
section.p: The ant's chart sends forage to the world and waits for arrive or found. The world is a JavaScript object on this page that picks each destination.
This page runs each colony as a host in its own Web Worker, so the browser can use two CPU cores.

section.heading: The same world runs in Node.js.
section.p: With a simulated clock and a fixed seed, every run prints the same five minutes of both colonies.
